assessment.nobel_worthiness: The lattice-trapped neutral-atom clock, with Katori's magic-wavelength idea removing the light shift, opened a new regime of precision in which frequency is controlled to the 10^-18 level. It is a clear, original and fundamental advance that I can explain with a simple picture: atoms held in light that does not disturb the transition being counted. It is already used for relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and the prospect of redefining the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength optical lattice and demonstrated it with strontium; Ye's group brought the lattice clock to record stability and accuracy and developed the many-body and comb-linked implementation. Two laureates give a clean configuration. Other strontium and ytterbium groups contributed important refinements and are not credited here, so the boundary of the credit is a judgement call.
assessment.maturity: Many independent laboratories on several continents have reproduced and surpassed the early results, and agreement between clocks is checked directly by comparison. The interpretation is stable and the timing is good, since the field has plainly matured while the redefinition of the second is still in progress.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to wait for the formal redefinition of the second before recognising the work.
Overlap with earlier recognition of frequency combs and ion-clock work (2005 and 2012 prizes) may make some colleagues see this as incremental.
My recollection of the details of who first demonstrated which clock species is from memory and I have not verified it.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Loading ultracold atoms into optical lattices lets one realise Hubbard-type models with tunable parameters, as in the observed superfluid to Mott-insulator transition, and then image the many-body state site by site. This gives direct, controlled access to quantum many-body questions that cannot be calculated or isolated in solids. It is a genuinely new way to ask fundamental questions, not just a technology.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Jaksch supplied the theoretical proposal for Hubbard physics in lattices; Greiner and Bloch carried out the Mott transition experiment and the quantum-gas microscope era; Esslinger's fermionic Hubbard and Fermi-surface work is also major. Cirac is credited elsewhere in the field but is more naturally linked to the quantum-simulation proposals. The five credited names exceed the three-person limit, so some excellent contributors are necessarily left out and my choice is debatable.
assessment.maturity: The results have been reproduced by many laboratories for two decades, with quantitative theory and experiment agreeing on Mott physics, and the field has matured into single-site-resolved studies. The recognition is not premature, though the 2001 BEC prize and the 2012 prize for quantum control of single particles partly cover neighbouring ground.
uncertainties: Which of Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger is most decisive for the experimental side is not settled.
Zoller also appears on several other candidates, which could complicate how a prize configuration is shared across fields.
I have not independently checked the priority of the individual lattice proposals.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Anyons are a conceptually striking discovery: in two dimensions particles need not be bosons or fermions, and fractionally charged excitations in the fractional quantum Hall liquid carry exactly this exotic exchange statistics. The theoretical idea is simple and deep, and it speaks to the question of what quantum statistics can be. Direct measurements of fractional charge by shot noise and of anyonic exchange statistics in collider and interferometer experiments give the idea physical content.
assessment.attribution: Leinaas and Myrheim's 1977 paper is the original statement of intermediate statistics in low dimensions; Heiblum's group made the decisive shot-noise measurement of fractional charge and the later interferometric work. Fève's collider experiments and Manfra's ultra-clean heterostructures are significant for the recent braiding confirmations. Wilczek's naming and the Arovas, Schrieffer and Wilczek Berry-phase calculation are not among the credited names, which leaves a hole in a fair attribution.
assessment.maturity: Fractional charge is solidly confirmed. Anyonic braiding has now been seen independently in electronic interferometers and in collider geometries, but the interpretation of some interferometry has been contested and refined, so confirmation is strong but still sharpening.
uncertainties: Without Wilczek, Arovas, Schrieffer or Halperin in the credited list the theoretical credit looks incomplete.
The Laughlin, Tsui and Stormer prize in 1998 covers the underlying fractional quantum Hall state, so the committee may want a sharper separation.
The independence and interpretation of recent braiding experiments are still being debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The recognition that band structure can carry a topological invariant protected by time-reversal symmetry, with conducting edge states, was an unexpected organising idea. The quantum spin Hall prediction and its observation in HgTe quantum wells are a direct link between a mathematical concept and a measured conductance. Its influence on materials, photonics and cold atoms is broad.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele proposed the Z2 quantum spin Hall insulator; Molenkamp's group observed the edge conductance in HgTe wells following the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposal. Hasan's three-dimensional topological insulator observations are also decisive, but the cap at three laureates forces a choice. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (not credited here) and Fu and Kane's three-dimensional theory make the allocation contested.
assessment.maturity: The field is well confirmed by several independent groups, with robust quantised measurements in HgTe and spectroscopy of the Bi-based materials. The 2016 prize for topological phase transitions covers part of the territory, so timing is reasonable but there is overlap.
uncertainties: Choosing between Molenkamp and Hasan for the experimental credit is not clear-cut.
The missing Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang prediction complicates fairness to the theorists.
This is condensed matter, where I defer to colleagues on the finer priority questions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Strong, controllable interactions between Rydberg atoms, which I know well from atomic structure, give a blockade that turns neutral atoms in optical tweezers into programmable arrays for quantum simulation and gates. The combination of a deep atomic-physics mechanism with clean quantum many-body experiments is impressive. It is attractive as fundamental science, though some of the appeal is tied to quantum computing, which is not my main criterion.
assessment.attribution: Lukin, Jaksch, Cirac and Zoller proposed the blockade for quantum information; Browaeys and Grangier showed the blockade between individual atoms; Saffman worked on gates; Lukin's group built large programmable arrays. The credit among Lukin, Browaeys, Saffman and Zoller is plausible but not clear-cut, and Bernien, Endres and Lahaye also contributed.
assessment.maturity: Results have been reproduced across groups and the platform is advancing quickly, but the best demonstrations are recent and fault-tolerant claims are still developing. I think it is somewhat early.
uncertainties: The field is still evolving and the lasting scientific discovery may be clearer in a decade.
Credit for the original blockade proposal against the later array experiments is divided.
Zoller's appearance on several candidates complicates the configuration.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle and the observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity opened a whole new platform for strongly correlated physics in a single tunable material. It is surprising and the control knob, the twist angle, is wonderfully simple to explain. Whether the physics itself is fully understood is another matter.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the quantitative prediction of the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero and collaborators observed the correlated insulator and superconductivity; Andrei's group contributed early scanning-probe evidence of flat bands. The inclusion of four names with a three-laureate cap leaves Andrei out, and I am not sure the credit between her and Jarillo-Herrero is cleanly separable.
assessment.maturity: Many groups reproduce the correlated phases, but the origin of the superconductivity and sample-to-sample variability are still debated. The interpretation is not yet stable, which makes me hesitate on timeliness.
uncertainties: The microscopic mechanism of superconductivity is unresolved.
Sample dependence and twist-angle disorder complicate the claim of a robust universal picture.
Credit is divided between theory and several experimental groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms demonstrates quantum superposition of massive objects and uses it to measure gravity, rotation and fundamental constants with high precision. It speaks to the boundary between the quantum and classical worlds, which I care about, and it provides precise tests of relativity and the equivalence principle. The work builds on laser cooling and the Ramsey method that were already honoured, and that lowers the sense of novelty somewhat.
assessment.attribution: Bordé introduced the theory of the atom interferometer with laser pulses, Pritchard's group built early atom interferometers with gratings and light, and Kasevich and Chu demonstrated the light-pulse gravimeter. Steven Chu is not in the credited names, which is a notable gap, and Chu already has a prize, so a fair configuration is not obvious.
assessment.maturity: The technique is robust, widely reproduced, and used in field instruments and large-baseline tests. The fundamental physics results are a continuing programme rather than a single completed discovery, so the recognition would be of the method.
uncertainties: Chu and Chu-related work is missing from the credited names, complicating attribution.
Whether the committee considers this a discovery or an instrument.
Precision tests have not yet shown a new effect, which weakens the case for a prize now.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Tuning the interaction between fermionic atoms with a Feshbach resonance from weakly paired BCS pairs to tightly bound molecular condensates showed the same quantum fluid across a continuous crossover, with the unitary gas being a remarkably universal system. The atomic physics is elegant and the connection to superconductors and neutron matter is fundamental. It is a case where theory and experiment meet at the percent level.
assessment.attribution: Thomas first observed strongly interacting Fermi gas behaviour, Grimm and Jin and Ketterle made molecular condensates and the crossover, and Salomon's group measured thermodynamics and the equation of state. Deborah Jin, who was central, died in 2016 and is not in the credited names, and Ketterle already holds a prize, so a fair allocation among the living credited names is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: The results are very well confirmed, with several laboratories agreeing on universal thermodynamics, but the discovery is now two decades old and its recognition is somewhat overdue relative to the lack of Jin. The remaining open questions concern the pseudogap regime.
uncertainties: The absence of Deborah Jin from the credited names makes a fair attribution difficult.
Overlap with the 2001 BEC prize and the surrounding ultracold-gas work could weigh against it.
I have not verified the precise ordering of the first observations in different laboratories.
